claims.text: At low applied fields, the magnetocaloric response of rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys is governed by an interplay between compositional disorder and magnetic exchange interactions.
Controlling the relative concentrations of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic elements can optimize magnetic exchange interactions and produce a near-critical magnetic phase transition.
Adjusting the relative concentrations of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic elements will shift the alloy closer to a critical magnetic phase transition.
Compositional disorder creates localized variations in magnetic exchange interactions.
Localized variations in magnetic exchange interactions enable the alloy to approach a critical magnetic phase transition.
Approaching a critical magnetic phase transition enhances the magnetocaloric effect.
The distributed nature of the magnetic phase transition maintains low hysteresis.
The distributed nature of the magnetic phase transition maintains mechanical stability.
The adjusted alloy will exhibit a stronger magnetocaloric response below 1 T than the baseline alloy.
The adjusted alloy will exhibit minimal hysteresis relative to the baseline composition.
The adjusted alloy will retain stable mechanical properties relative to the baseline composition.
The proposed relationship should hold near room temperature and below 1 T for rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys having similar compositional disorder and magnetic exchange characteristics.
Failure of adjusted compositions to improve the low-field magnetocaloric response, or an accompanying increase in hysteresis or loss of mechanical stability, would falsify the hypothesis.
